blocks.heading: CHAPTER 4 — What Do You Want? — Shū biddak? | شو بدّك؟
paragraphs: In the last chapter, you learned how to talk about what exists, what you have, and where things are. You’ve already built a solid foundation for describing the world around you. Now we’re going to make things a little more personal. We’re going to learn how to talk about what you want.

Think about how often you express what you want throughout the day. Maybe you want a cup of coffee, a bigger apartment, a new phone, or just a little peace and quiet. Maybe someone asks what you want for dinner, or you need to explain that you don’t want something. These are simple conversations, but they’re also some of the most useful ones you’ll have in everyday life.
That’s what this chapter is all about.

You’ll learn how to express what you want, ask other people what they want, and explain what you don’t want. We’ll also explore how to talk about things you wanted in the past or might want in the future.
But we’re not going to stop there.

So far, you’ve mostly been working with shorter sentences. In this chapter, we’ll start bringing those ideas together. You’ll learn how to connect your thoughts, explain your preferences, and express more than one idea at a time. Instead of simply saying that you want something, you’ll be able to explain that you want it but don’t have it, or that you want one thing and something else.

As you work through the lessons, you’ll see how much you can already say with the Arabic you’ve learned. We’re not starting over or suddenly introducing a completely different way of speaking. We’re taking what you already know and giving you more ways to use it.

By the end of this chapter, you’ll be able to have more meaningful everyday conversations about your wants, needs, and preferences. More importantly, you’ll be able to put your thoughts together in a way that sounds increasingly natural.
The goal isn’t just to learn how to say “I want.” It’s to give you more freedom to express yourself in Arabic.

blocks.heading: CHAPTER 4 | Everyday Expression — God willing / hopefully! — إن شاء الله | in shāʾ Allāh
blocks.text:
You will hear إن شاء الله constantly in Arabic. Literally, it means if God wills, but in everyday conversation, it often feels like:
“God willing.”
“Hopefully.”
“If everything works out.”
This expression fits naturally here because you are learning how to talk about what you want with بِدّ. When people talk about hopes, plans, wants, or future situations, إن شاء الله comes up all the time.
Sometimes people joke that إن شاء الله can mean “probably not” or “that’s never going to happen.” And yes, people do sometimes use it that way, depending on tone and context.
But most of the time, people use it in its basic sense, acknowledging that the future is not fully in our hands. It shows humility, hope, and the belief that what happens is ultimately in God’s hands.

blocks.heading: Here’s how it looks in context:
Main idea
blocks.text: Use إن شاء الله when you are talking about something you hope will happen or something you plan for, but you know it is not fully guaranteed. It is one of the most common expressions in Arabic, and it helps your speech sound more natural, polite, and culturally connected.

items.notes: Note: We use كافيه (kāfēh) because it’s what most people say for a café. In everyday Levantine speech, القَهْوة (il-ʾahwe, “the coffee”) can also mean “the café” or “the coffee shop”; context tells you whether it refers to the drink or the place. On signs and in writing, you will also see مَقْهى (maqhā).
Note: We use دُكّانة (dukkāne) for a small neighborhood grocery or corner shop. You may also hear بَقّالة (baqqāle) for a grocery shop. سوبرماركت (sūbarmārkit) refers to a supermarket.

Note: مَكْتَبة (maktabe) can mean either “library” or “bookstore.” The intended meaning depends on context. If someone is borrowing books, they are probably referring to a library. If they are buying books, they are referring to a bookstore.

Note: مَرْكَز شُرْطة (markaz shurṭa) is a general term for “police station.” In Palestinian Arabic, مَخْفَر (makhfar) is also commonly used for a local police station or police post. In Jordan, you will frequently hear مَرْكَز أَمْني (markaz amnī), another common term for a police station.

flags.note: Arabic جامِعة is voweled with kasra on م (jāmiʿa) but the singular transliteration is jāmʿa; plural shows jāmiʿāt.

items.notes: Note: We use جَوّال (jawwāl) as our primary term for “cell phone.” In Palestine, جوّال is also the name of the first Palestinian mobile operator, which launched in 1999. In Jordan, you’ll also commonly hear موبايل (mōbāyl). These terms are not exclusive to either country.
Note: أَواعي (awāʿi) is common in Jordanian/Palestinian Arabic; تياب (tyāb) is also widely common in both places and used across the Levant.
Note: بِطاقة هُوِيّة (biṭāʾet huwiyye) means “ID card”; in everyday speech, الهُوِيّة (il-huwiyye) is usually enough.
Note: مَصاري (maṣāri, “money”) is plural in form. In everyday speech, words referring back to it may be plural or feminine singular.
Shoes: In this book, كُنْدَرة (kundara) means a pair of shoes, and كَنادِر (kanādir) is its plural. To specify one single shoe, use فَرْد كُنْدَرة (fard kundara).

Note: عِدّة (ʿidde) is a collective noun commonly used to refer to tools or equipment as a group. Although grammatically singular, it can refer to multiple tools. Its plural, عِدَد (ʿidad), is generally used when referring to multiple sets of tools or equipment.
Note: In formal writing, this word is spelled نظيف with ظ. In everyday Levantine Arabic, the ظ is pronounced more like ض, so this book writes it the way it sounds: نْضيف (nḍīf).
Note: قَريبين (ʾarībīn) is the plural taught here; قْراب (ʾrāb) is another common plural you may hear.

Note: In everyday Palestinian and Jordanian Arabic, you may hear both بْعاد (bʿād) and بْعيدين (bʿīdīn) as plural forms of بْعيد (bʿīd), meaning “far” or “distant.” بْعاد is a broken plural, while بْعيدين uses the regular plural ending ـين (-īn). Both forms are useful to recognize in conversation.

Note: In everyday Palestinian and Jordanian Arabic, صْغير (ẓghīr) is often pronounced with a Z-like sound rather than the standard Arabic Ṣ sound. You may also see it written colloquially as زْغير. Both spellings refer to the same adjective, meaning “small” or “young.” Pronunciation varies by region and speaker.

blocks.text: Note: The plural adjective forms listed here are not limited to people. In everyday Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic, plural nouns referring to things or places may take either a plural adjective or a feminine singular adjective. Usage varies with the noun, the adjective, the speaker, and the context.

blocks.heading: 4.1 Wanting
paragraphs: In this chapter, we will be dealing with one of the most frequently used expressions in Levantine Arabic: بِدُّه | biddo

بِدّ (bidd-) is how you say “want.” You will learn how to form it for all persons, how to say what you want, how to negate it (and how negation works with similar possession expressions), and how to express these ideas in the past and future.

blocks.heading: Attaching the Person
paragraphs: bidd- uses the same person endings you already know from possession expressions like عِند (ʿind-) and مَع (maʿ-). Attach the appropriate ending to show who wants something.
Here are all the forms:
The personal pronoun (e.g., أنا، هو، هي, etc.) is not necessary, because bidd- already tells you who the subject is. You can still add the pronoun if you want, especially for emphasis. For example:
أنا بدّي قهوة (ana biddī ʾahwe) means “I want coffee,” but بدّي قهوة (biddī ʾahwe) already sounds complete and natural.

blocks.heading: Here’s how it looks in context:

items.en: She wants a cup of cold water
Do you want some hot tea?

blocks.heading: 💡 Remember
blocks.text: These are the same person endings you already know from عِند (ʿind-) and مَع (maʿ-). If you know عِندي كتاب (ʿindī ktāb), “I have a book,” then بِدّي كتاب (biddī ktāb), “I want a book,” follows a familiar pattern.

blocks.title: What Do You Want? Drill
blocks.instructions:
You already know how to use بِدّ (bidd) to talk about what someone wants. In this drill, your main goal is to choose the correct form of بِدّ (bidd) for each person.
At first, the answers are short and simple. As the drill continues, you will be asked to say a little more by adding familiar vocabulary, places, and short descriptions. Do not let the longer answers distract you from the main target: getting the form of بِدّ (bidd) correct.
Some later sentences include اللّي (illī, “that/which”), which you will study in Section 4.5. For now, focus on the correct form of بِدّ; you do not need to use اللّي yourself yet.
As the drill progresses, you’ll also use مِن (min), “from,” to connect items with the places they come from.
Read each question out loud, fill in the blank, and then say the entire answer out loud. Even when the answer becomes longer, keep listening for the rhythm of بِدّ (bidd) at the beginning.
Say everything out loud. Repetition is your friend.

blocks.heading: 4.2 Wanting “It”
paragraphs: Up to this point, you’ve learned how to say that you want something. For example:
بِدّي قَهْوِة — biddī ʾahwe — I want coffee.
But in real conversation, we do not always repeat the same noun.
In English, once the thing is already clear, we replace the noun with a pronoun:
I want the coffee. → I want it.
I want the car. → I want it.
I want the books. → I want them.
Arabic works the same way. Once the thing has already been mentioned or is clear from context, you can replace the noun with an object pronoun.
Use إيّاه with masculine singular nouns, إيّاها with feminine singular nouns, and إيّاهم with plural nouns. With plural things, you’ll also hear إيّاها (iyyāha).

blocks.heading: Formula: بِدّ + person ending + إيّاه / إيّاها / إيّاهم
Gender and Number
paragraphs: The object pronoun follows the gender and number of the noun it refers back to.

blocks.heading: When Do You Use It?
paragraphs: Use this structure when the noun has already been mentioned or is obvious from context. Imagine walking into a bookstore and speaking to one of the employees:

items.translit: biddī il-ktāb il-jdīd tabaʿ Jalāl Barjas
items.en: “I want the new book by Jalal Barjas. . .”

paragraphs: The second sentence works because everyone already knows that إيّاه (iyyāh) refers to the book.
If the listener does not know what you are talking about, use the noun first.

blocks.heading: One more natural pattern
paragraphs: In spoken Levantine Arabic, you will also commonly hear the thing someone wants placed at the beginning of the sentence and then referred back to with إيّاه (iyyāh), إيّاها (iyyāha), or إيّاهم (iyyāhum).
This lets the speaker bring the thing being talked about to the front and emphasize it:
[Mentioned noun] + بِدّ (bidd-) + person ending + إيّاه / إيّاها / إيّاهم
The form of بِدّ changes according to who wants something. The object pronoun changes according to the gender and number of the thing being wanted.

blocks.title: The "I Want It" Drill
blocks.instructions:
You learned how to talk about possession in the previous chapter. Now you are going to connect those structures with بِدّ (bidd) and the object pronouns إيّاه / إيّاها / إيّاهم (iyyāh / iyyāha / iyyāhum).
For each item, read the English sentence first. Then fill in the first blank with the correct noun or noun phrase. Some of these phrases include possession, so pay attention to the entire meaning of the English sentence.
Next, fill in the second blank with إيّاه (iyyāh), إيّاها (iyyāha), or إيّاهم (iyyāhum). The answer key gives model answers; alternatives explicitly accepted in the chapter notes are also acceptable. Remember that the object pronoun matches the gender and number of the Arabic noun—not the person who wants it. For example, مَصاري (money) is plural in form, while عِدّة (tools/equipment) is feminine singular. Follow the Arabic noun even when English groups things differently.
Say the entire exchange out loud after filling in both blanks. The goal is to connect vocabulary, possession, and object pronouns until you can quickly hear whether you need إيّاه (iyyāh), إيّاها (iyyāha), or إيّاهم (iyyāhum).
Say everything out loud. Repetition is your friend.

blocks.heading: 4.3 Negation of Desire
paragraphs: To say that you do not want something, put the negative particle مَا (mā) before the entire بِدّ (bidd) expression.

This should already feel familiar. You have used مَا (mā) to negate several structures from previous chapters, including possession with عِنْد (ʿind), مَع (maʿ), and إلـ (il-), as well as مَا في (mā fī) to say that something does not exist or is not there.
The same basic pattern applies here:
مَا + بِدّ with the appropriate person suffix + noun / object pronoun
You have also learned مِش (mish) as a way to say “not,” but بِدّ (bidd) is not normally negated with مِش (mish). Instead, use مَا (mā):
مَا بِدّي قَهْوِة — mā biddī ʾahwe — I do not want coffee
This use of مَا (mā) will become even more important later when you begin working with verbs.

items.en: she does not want a car

paragraphs: The pattern stays the same whether you name the object directly or replace it with إِيّاه، إِيّاها، or إِيّاهم (iyyāh, iyyāha, iyyāhum).
In everyday speech, you may also hear reduced pronunciations such as yāh, yāha, and yāhum. These refer to the same object-pronoun forms.
To negate the entire expression, place ما (mā) before بِدّ (bidd) and keep the rest of the sentence unchanged.

blocks.heading: The Colloquial ـش Ending
paragraphs: In everyday Palestinian and Jordanian Arabic, you may also hear negative expressions formed with ـش (-sh).
These forms are common in some regional and conversational varieties, but their frequency varies by speaker and dialect. The plain form, ما بِدّي (mā biddī), is just as natural.

For this book, we will learn both patterns so you can recognize either one in conversation. When completing the drills, either form is acceptable unless a question specifies otherwise. Here are the forms:
مَا (mā) + بِدّ (bidd-) + person ending + ـش (-sh)
Start with the correct form of بِدّ for the person you’re talking about. Then add ـش to make the colloquial negative form.

blocks.heading: Here’s how it looks in context:

items.en: We do not want a big house
She does not want a nearby apartment

blocks.heading: Quick Speech Note
blocks.text:
In some varieties, you may hear negation with only the ـش ending, without ما.
بِدّيش | I do not want – biddīsh
بِدّهاش | She does not want – biddhāsh
These forms still express negation. Their use depends on the speaker and variety of Arabic, not simply on how formal or informal the situation is.

blocks.heading: Same Ending with Possession
paragraphs: You can also add the same ـش ending to possession structures like عند and مع.

items.en: she does not have it with her
he does not have it with him

paragraphs: Just like with بِدّ, both patterns express negation. Which form you hear depends on the speaker and variety of Arabic, not simply on the formality of the situation.

blocks.title: Colloquial Negation Drill
blocks.instructions:
Part A — Saying What You Don’t Want
You’ve already learned how to say what someone wants using بِدّ. Now let’s practice saying what someone doesn’t want.
In everyday Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic, there are two common ways to express this:
ما بِدّي قَهْوة | I don’t want coffee — mā biddī ʾahwe
ما بِدّيش قَهْوة | I don’t want coffee — mā biddīsh ʾahwe
Both forms are acceptable in this drill. Use whichever feels more comfortable, but practice saying both out loud.
Complete each sentence with the correct negative expression. As you progress, you’ll also review possession, familiar vocabulary, and other structures from earlier chapters.
Say everything out loud. Repetition is your friend.
Part B — Everyday Situations (items 8–15)
Now we’ll add a little more context.
Sometimes you’ll simply refuse something. Other times, you’ll explain a preference or say that someone doesn’t have something.
Remember that negation works with familiar possession expressions such as عِنْد and مَع, too.
Part C — Negation and Vocabulary (items 16–23)
Now let’s take things a little further.
So far, you’ve practiced choosing the correct negative expression. This time, you’ll also need to remember the vocabulary that belongs in each sentence.
Complete the missing negative expression and noun using the English as your guide. Notice how the sentences connect ideas through reasons, preferences, and conjunctions. You may see words like عَشان (because), لَأَنّه (because), and بَسّ (but) before their full lesson in Section 4.6. For now, recognize what they mean; the blanks test negation and vocabulary, not the conjunctions.
You may use either ما بِدّ or ما بِدّ…ش.
Part D — Putting It Together (items 24–30)
Now let’s combine everything you’ve practiced.
Some sentences use negative desire with بِدّ, while others use negative possession with عِنْد or مَع. You’ll also need to supply the correct noun. Each negative possession expression fits in one blank.
Pay attention to how the sentences express reasons and connect ideas. Think about what each person actually means rather than treating the blanks as separate words.
Read the completed sentences out loud.

lessons.title: Past and Future: Desire and Possession

blocks.heading: 4.4 Past and Future: Desire and Possession
paragraphs: You have already used كَان في (kān fī) and رَح يْكون في (raḥ ykūn fī) to talk about what existed or will exist. Now we will use the same frames with عِنْد (ʿind) and بِدّ (bidd).
For now, keep كَان (kān) and رَح يْكون (raḥ ykūn) fixed. The pronoun suffix attached to بِدّ (bidd) or عِنْد (ʿind) tells you who wanted, had, is going to want, or is going to have something.
The goal is simple: take familiar desire and possession structures and move them naturally between the past and future.

blocks.heading: Past Desire and Possession
paragraphs: To talk about what someone wanted or had in the past, place كَان (kān) directly before the familiar بِدّ (bidd) or عِنْد (ʿind) structure.

items.en: She had a big house in the suburbs

blocks.heading: Past Negation
paragraphs: For now, keep كَان (kān) fixed. The pronoun suffix attached to بِدّ (bidd) or عِنْد (ʿind) identifies the person.
To make the past structure negative, place مَا (mā) before كَان (kān).
Formula: mā (مَا) + kān (كَان) + bidd- (بِدّ) / ʿind- (عِنْد) + suffix

items.ar: مَا كَان بِدّها إِشي مِن المَحَلّ
items.translit: mā kān biddha ishi min il-maḥall
items.en: She did not want anything from the store
I did not have time today

paragraphs: The important thing is the position of مَا (mā). It comes before كَان (kān) because the entire past structure is negative.

blocks.heading: Moving into the Future
paragraphs: To talk about what someone is going to want or have, place رَح يْكون (raḥ ykūn) before the familiar بِدّ (bidd) or عِنْد (ʿind) structure.

items.en: He is going to want a new car

items.ar: رَح يْكون بِدّها غَدا بَعْد التَّمْرين
items.translit: raḥ ykūn biddha ghada baʿd it-tamrīn
items.en: She is going to want lunch after the workout
He is going to have a new key

items.ar: رَح يْكون عِنْدها شُغْل كْتير بُكْرا
items.translit: raḥ ykūn ʿindha shughl ktīr bukra
items.en: She is going to have a lot of work tomorrow
I am going to have a question later

blocks.heading: Future Negation
paragraphs: To make the future structure negative, place مَا (mā) before رَح يْكون (raḥ ykūn).
Formula: mā (مَا) + raḥ ykūn (رَح يْكون) + bidd- (بِدّ) / ʿind- (عِنْد) + suffix

items.en: I am not going to have time
He is not going to want coffee

blocks.heading: Main Idea — To move desire or possession into the past or future, place the correct time frame before بِدّ (bidd) or عِنْد (ʿind).
rows: mā (مَا) + raḥ ykūn (رَح يْكون) + bidd- (بِدّ) / ʿind- (عِنْد) + suffix

paragraphs: To make either structure negative, place مَا (mā) at the beginning.
The time frame tells you when. The pronoun suffix attached to بِدّ (bidd) or عِنْد (ʿind) tells you who.

blocks.title: Past and Future: Desire and Possession Drill
blocks.instructions:
Instructions: Fill in the blanks to complete each sentence.
In this drill, you’ll practice expressing both desire and possession in the past and future.
Past Desire: كان + بِدّ (kān + bidd)
Future Desire: رَح يْكون + بِدّ (raḥ ykūn + bidd)
Past Possession: كان + عِنْد (kān + ʿind)
Future Possession: رَح يْكون + عِنْد (raḥ ykūn + ʿind)
Remember: The person ending attached to بِدّ or عِنْد tells you who wants or has something. For negative sentences, place ما before كان or رح يكون.
The drill becomes progressively more difficult. At first, you’ll complete the appropriate structure. As you progress, familiar vocabulary will begin disappearing too. By the end, you’ll be rebuilding larger parts of the sentence using structures you’ve already learned.
Some sentences use اللّي (illī, “that”), which you’ll study in 4.5. Read the English first and say each sentence out loud.
Say everything out loud. Repetition is your friend.

blocks.drillName: Past and Future: Desire and Possession Drill

blocks.heading: 4.5 Identifying the One You Mean — اللّي | illī
paragraphs: Sometimes saying “the phone,” “the bag,” or “the coffee” is not specific enough. There may be several phones, bags, or coffees, so you need a way to show which one you mean.
To do this, we can use what is grammatically called a relative pronoun. A relative pronoun connects a noun to extra information that identifies or describes it.
In Levantine Arabic, one very useful word for adding that identifying information is:
that / which / who — illī | اللّي

Think of اللّي (illī) as the word that connects a specific noun to extra information that tells us which one you mean. اللّي does not change its form. The same word can be used with people, objects, masculine nouns, feminine nouns, singular nouns, and plurals.

For now, we will use اللّي after definite nouns—when we’re talking about a specific person or thing. This is the pattern you’ll practice in this section. Later, you’ll encounter other ways of connecting descriptions to nouns.
The basic pattern
definite noun + اللّي + identifying information

items.en: the book that is on the table

items.note: Then add the information that identifies it:

items.en: the book that is on the table

blocks.heading: The same pattern works with other nouns:

items.en: the bag that is next to the door
the phone that is with me

blocks.heading: SECTION 4.5
paragraphs: Sometimes you need more information about the thing someone means. A useful question is:
shū nōʿ …? | شو نوع…؟ What kind / type of …?
Here, نوع (type/kind) forms an iḍāfa structure with the noun that follows it, giving the meaning “type of [that noun].”

items.en: the coffee that has sugar in it

paragraphs: In the answer, اللّي adds the information that identifies the specific coffee  being discussed. So, شو نوع…؟ gives us another reason to use the same pattern:
definite noun + اللّي + identifying information
You ask for more information, and اللّي helps provide it.

blocks.heading: One Important Thing to Notice
paragraphs: Look at this question:
شو نوع الشَّنْطة اللّي بِدَّك إِيّاها؟ — shū nōʿ ish-shanṭa illī biddak iyyāha? — What kind of bag do you want?
Notice that إِيّاها (iyyāha) refers to الشَّنْطة (ish-shanṭa), not نَوْع (nōʿ). Because شَنْطة is feminine, we use the feminine object pronoun إِيّاها.
The pattern is:
شو نوع + definite noun + اللّي + identifying information
When an object pronoun is needed, match it to the noun being identified. Remember that اللّي itself never changes for gender or number.

blocks.heading: اللّي Does Not Change
paragraphs: One useful thing about اللّي is that it stays the same whether the noun is masculine, feminine, singular, or plural.

items.en: the phone that is in the store
the bag that is in the store
the shoes that are in the store

blocks.title: What Kind is That Drill: Part 1
blocks.instructions:
Part A — Identifying the One You Mean
You’ve already learned how to describe people and things using adjectives, locations, and possession. Now let’s put those skills together with اللّي (illī).
Remember, اللّي connects a specific noun to additional information that helps identify which person or thing you mean.
In this drill, you’ll need to supply both the definite noun and اللّي.
For example:
I want the bag that’s next to the door.
بِدّي ________ ________ جَنْب الباب.
biddī ________ ________ janb il-bāb.
Answer: الشَّنْطة / اللّي — ish-shanṭa / illī
Use the English to identify the missing vocabulary. Pay attention to definiteness, gender, and the information that follows اللّي.
Say everything out loud. Repetition is your friend.
Part A — Continued (items 9–15)
Keep using the same pattern: a definite noun followed by اللّي and the information that identifies it.
Notice that the sentences now bring together several things you’ve already learned, including possession, descriptions, and preferences.

lessons.title: Conjunctions — ḥurūf il-ʿaṭf | حروف العطف (F, A, N, B)

blocks.heading: 4.6 Conjunctions — ḥurūf il-ʿaṭf | حروف العطف
paragraphs: All right, let’s take a little trip back to grade school and revisit a familiar concept: conjunctions. A conjunction is a word that connects words, phrases, or ideas together. You may remember learning a group of common English conjunctions with the acronym FANBOYS:
For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So

These little words help connect ideas and make sentences flow more naturally. Arabic does the same thing, but there is one important difference: the Arabic conjunctions do not always line up perfectly with English.
What matters most is understanding the job each conjunction is doing in the sentence. Is it adding information, giving a reason, showing contrast, offering a choice, or showing a result?
Once you start recognizing those relationships between ideas, the Arabic conjunctions become much easier to use naturally.
Let’s start with F — For.

blocks.heading: F — For: Giving a Reason
paragraphs: In FANBOYS, for does not mean “for someone.” Here, for means something closer to because or for this reason.
For example:
The store is closed, for the front door is broken.
That sounds a little formal in modern English. We would normally say:
The store is closed because the front door is broken.
So the important idea here is simple:
We are giving a reason.
In Southern Levantine Arabic, we will focus on two common ways to do this:

blocks.heading: عَشان / مِنشان — Everyday “because / because of”
paragraphs: عشان and مِنشان essentially mean the same thing. Both are very common in Southern Levantine Arabic. Some speakers may use عَشان more often, while others may prefer مِنشان, depending on the region and the speaker.
For this book, you can treat them as interchangeable ways of expressing the same basic idea. Neither one is more correct than the other.
It can help to see where these expressions come from:
So, very literally:
عَلى + شَأْن → عَشان — something like “on account of the matter”
مِن + شَأْن → مِنشان — something like “from / because of the matter”

You do not need to translate these pieces separately when you speak. In everyday Levantine Arabic, عَشان and مِنشان function as complete expressions and are commonly used to mean because, because of, or for.

items.en: He is at home because the school is closed

items.note: They can also come directly before a noun or noun phrase:

paragraphs: For now, the main idea is simple: عَشان and مِنشان both introduce a reason or purpose.

blocks.heading: لَأَنُّه — “Because” + a Reason
paragraphs: لَأَنّه is another very common way to explain why something is true. It introduces the reason or explanation that follows.

items.ar: الجَواب مِش واضِح لَأَنّه السُؤال صَعِب.
items.translit: il-jawāb mish wāḍiḥ laʾanno is-suʾāl ṣaʿib.
items.en: The answer is not clear because the question is difficult.
The store is closed because the door is broken.
She is at home because the car is broken.

items.ar: المَحَلّ مْسَكّر لَأَنّه الباب القُدّامي مَكْسور.
items.translit: il-maḥall msakkar laʾanno il-bāb il-ʾuddāmi maksūr.
items.en: The store is closed because the front door is broken.
items.note: A useful pattern is: idea + لَأَنّه + reason

paragraphs: For now, learn لَأَنّه as one complete connector meaning because.
You may also hear related forms such as:
You do not need to memorize these forms yet. We will come back to them later.

blocks.heading: Which One Should You Use?
paragraphs: There is a lot of overlap between عَشان / مِنشان and لَأَنّه, but they are not used in exactly the same way.
The easiest difference to remember is:
عَشان / مِنشان can come before either: a complete clause, or a noun / noun phrase
لَأَنّه normally needs a complete clause after it.
Here, الشُّغْل is just a noun phrase. There is no complete sentence after عشان / منشان, and that is perfectly natural.
❌ لَأَنّه الشُّغْل

لَأَنّه usually introduces a reason expressed as a complete clause. When you’re simply giving a noun phrase as the reason, عَشان or مِنشان is generally the easier and more natural choice for the patterns we’re practicing.

blocks.heading: So for now, remember:
blocks.text:
عَشان / مِنشان — can introduce either a noun phrase or a complete clause
لَأَنّه — normally introduces a complete clause

blocks.heading: A — And: Adding Ideas
paragraphs: This one is nice and easy.
The most common way to say “and” in Arabic is:
و | and — w- / u
Use و to connect words, phrases, or ideas, just like English and.
In speech, و attaches directly to the word that comes after it.

blocks.heading: Connecting Items in a List
paragraphs: Depending on the surrounding sounds and the speaker, و may sound closer to w- or u-, but it is the same word.
Arabic often repeats وَ (w-) when listing several things.
In English, we might say:
A book, a notebook, and a pen.
In everyday Arabic, it's natural to connect each item with وَ:

items.en: A book, a notebook, and a pen.

paragraphs: Notice that Arabic uses وَ before both the second and third items.
The meaning is the same, but Arabic often makes the connections between items more explicit than English does.
Remember: وَ is a conjunction, not a comma. It simply connects one idea to another.

items.en: a cat, a dog, and a boy
a door, a table, and a chair
a brother, a sister, and a friend

paragraphs: Think of و as the little piece of glue connecting the items together.

blocks.heading: N — Nor: “Or” in a Negative Sentence
paragraphs: You probably do not use the word nor very often in everyday English. Arabic, however, uses this idea all the time. The key word is:
وَلا | nor; or in a negative sentence — wala
When an English sentence is negative, English often uses or:
He does not have a book or a pen.
In Southern Levantine Arabic, it is very natural to use وَلا:
ما عِنده كْتاب وَلا قَلَم | mā ʿindo ktāb wala ʾalam — He does not have a book or a pen.
You can think of وَلا here as:
and not … either
So the literal idea behind the sentence is “He does not have a book, and not a pen either”:
ما عِنده كْتاب وَلا قَلَم | mā ʿindo ktāb wala ʾalam — He does not have a book or a pen.

blocks.heading: A Useful Pattern
paragraphs: In Southern Levantine Arabic, وَلا (wala) is commonly used to connect two things within a negative statement.
The important thing to remember is that the first part of the sentence establishes the negation. Then وَلا introduces the second thing being excluded.
For example:

items.en: I don’t have coffee or tea
I don’t have a key or a cell phone with me

items.ar: ما بِدّي الغُرْفة الكْبيرة وَلا الصْغيرة
items.translit: mā biddī il-ghurfe il-kbīre wala iẓ-ẓghīre
items.en: I don’t want the big room or the small one

blocks.heading: Neither … Nor …
paragraphs: Notice that each sentence begins with a negative expression using ما. We don’t need to add لا before the first item because the sentence is already negative.
You may also hear the pattern:
لا … وَلا | neither … nor — lā … wala
For example:

blocks.heading: The Main Idea
paragraphs: This pattern is especially useful when listing two alternatives without an earlier negative expression.
Both patterns are useful:
ما + negative statement + وَلا + second alternative
لا + first alternative + وَلا + second alternative
The difference is where the negation begins.
For now, remember:
و | and — w-
وَلا | or / nor in a negative statement — wala
لا … وَلا | neither … nor — lā … wala
You don’t need to memorize two separate translations for وَلا. Just recognize that it adds another item to something being negated.

blocks.heading: B — But: Showing Contrast
paragraphs: The everyday spoken word for “but” is:
بَسّ | but — bass
Use بَسّ when the second idea contrasts with the first.
The first part gives one idea. بَسّ introduces a different idea, an opposite idea, or an unexpected turn.
A Useful Pattern
idea 1 + بَسّ + idea 2

items.en: The restaurant is expensive, but the food is delicious.
The picture is old, but beautiful.
The apartment is small, but the balcony is big.

paragraphs: Both ideas are true, but they pull in different directions.
For example:
The restaurant is expensive.
The food is delicious.
Put them together:
المَطْعَم غالي، بَسّ الأَكِل زاكي | il-maṭʿam ghāli, bass il-akil zāki — The restaurant is expensive, but the food is delicious.
You can also use بَسّ when describing one thing with two contrasting qualities:

items.en: The room is nice, but small.
The bag is clean, but old.
The work is important, but difficult.

blocks.heading: بَسّ Can Also Mean “Just / Only”
paragraphs: بَسّ can also mean “just” or “only.” In this use, it limits the meaning rather than showing contrast.
For now, remember:
بَسّ = but / just / only
The meaning is usually clear from context.

lessons.title: Conjunctions (continued): O — Or, Y — Yet, S — So

blocks.heading: O — Or: Giving a Choice
paragraphs: Southern Levantine Arabic has two very common ways to say “or”:
أَو | or — aw
وَلّا | or — walla
They both express alternatives, but they are commonly used in different situations.

blocks.heading: أَو | or — aw: A Neutral “Or”
paragraphs: Use أَو when you are simply connecting two alternatives or possibilities.
It is especially common in statements and when the speaker is not directly asking someone to choose.

blocks.heading: وَلّا “Or?” When Asking Someone to Choose
paragraphs: Think of أَو as the general, neutral word for “or.”
وَلّا (walla) is extremely common in spoken Levantine Arabic when you are directly asking someone to choose between two alternatives.
Before you go any further, pay close attention to one small detail:
وَلّا is especially associated with questions.
Think of it as the conversational “or?” in a question like:
“Coffee or tea?”
“This one or that one?”
“The restaurant or the café?”
For example:

items.en: Do you want coffee or tea?
Do you want this one or that one?

blocks.heading: SECTION 4.6
paragraphs: In each case, the speaker is presenting two possibilities and asking the listener to choose between them.
A useful way to think about it is:
choice A + وَلّا + choice B?
So when you hear وَلّا in a question, your brain should immediately expect an alternative or a choice.
This is different from simply joining two ideas together. وَلّا tells the listener:
“Which of these?”
For now, use وَلّا when you are directly presenting alternatives in a spoken question.

blocks.heading: Important: Watch the Shadda
blocks.text:
You just learned وَلا (wala) in the N — Nor section. Now you are learning وَلّا (walla).
وَلا | nor / or in a negative sentence — wala
وَلّا | or? / or in a direct choice question — walla
The shadda marks a doubled ل sound. In this book, we write وَلا (wala) for negative alternatives and وَلّا (walla) for direct-choice questions. Use the sentence context as well as the pronunciation to recognize the intended meaning.

items.en: I do not have coffee or tea.
Do you want coffee or tea?

blocks.heading: Now look at a few more examples of وَلّا:

items.en: Is the notebook new or old?
Is the door open or closed?

blocks.heading: Keep It Simple
blocks.text:
أَو → a neutral alternative
وَلّا → a direct “this or that?” question

items.en: Do you want coffee or tea?

paragraphs: The English word “or” is the same in both sentences, but the Arabic changes depending on what the speaker is doing.

blocks.heading: Y — Yet: A Stronger Contrast
paragraphs: Good news—you already know the main word you need here:
بَسّ | but; yet — bass
English sometimes uses “yet” where we could also say “but.” In everyday Southern Levantine Arabic, بَسّ usually works naturally for both.

items.en: The restaurant is expensive, yet the food is delicious.
The house is small, yet clean.
The room is small, yet nice.

paragraphs: So for now:
بَسّ = but / yet
The English translation may change, but the basic idea is the same: the second idea contrasts with the first.

blocks.heading: مَع هيك — “Even So / Nevertheless”
paragraphs: When you want a stronger contrast, you can use:
مَع هيك / ومَع هيك | even so; nevertheless; but still — maʿ hēk / w-maʿ hēk
It points back to the first idea and means something like: “Even though that is true...” Literally: “even with that.”

items.en: The apartment is expensive; even so, it is small.
The house is old; even so, it is clean.

blocks.heading: Keep It Simple
blocks.text:
بَسّ → but / yet; everyday contrast
مَع هيك → even so / nevertheless; stronger contrast

blocks.heading: S — So: Showing a Result — عَشان هيك / مِنشان هيك — “So / That’s Why”
paragraphs: In English, “so” often introduces a result. One situation comes first, and the next idea follows because of it.
You can think of the pattern like this:
X happened → so / therefore → Y is the result
For example:
The car is broken, so she is at home.
Southern Levantine Arabic often uses:
عَشان هيك | so; that’s why; for that reason — ʿashān hēk
مِنشان هيك | so; that’s why; for that reason — minshān hēk
Before looking at the full expressions, notice one word inside both of them:
هيك | like this; like that; this way — hēk
هيك points to a way, situation, or idea.
For example:
هَادا هيك | It is like this — hāda hēk
When we add عَشان or مِنشان, the expression points back to the situation that came before it:
عَشان هيك / مِنشان هيك
The idea is close to:
because of that / for that reason
In natural English, this often comes out simply as:
so / that’s why
Just like عَشان and مِنشان, عَشان هيك and مِنشان هيك essentially mean the same thing. Some speakers may prefer one over the other, but both are very common.

items.ar: السَيّارة خَرْبانة، عَشان هيك هِيِّ بِالبَيْت.
items.translit: is-sayyāra kharbāne, ʿashān hēk hiyye bil-bēt
items.en: The car is broken, so she is at home.

items.ar: السَيّارة خَرْبانة، مِنشان هيك هِيِّ بِالبَيْت.
items.translit: is-sayyāra kharbāne, minshān hēk hiyye bil-bēt
items.en: The car is broken, so she is at home.

items.ar: الباب مَكْسور، عَشان هيك المَحَلّ مْسَكَّر.
items.translit: il-bāb maksūr, ʿashān hēk il-maḥall msakkar
items.en: The door is broken, so the store is closed.

items.ar: السُّؤال صَعِب، مِنشان هيك الجَواب مِش واضِح.
items.translit: is-suʾāl ṣaʿib, minshān hēk il-jawāb mish wāḍiḥ
items.en: The question is difficult, so the answer is not clear.

paragraphs: A useful pattern is:
reason + عَشان هيك / مِنشان هيك + result
The first idea gives the reason or situation. عَشان هيك / مِنشان هيك then points back to it and introduces the result.

blocks.heading: فَ | so — fa: A Short “So / Then”
paragraphs: فَـ is a short connector that moves the sentence forward.
Think of it like a small arrow:
first idea → فَـ → what follows
The next idea may be:
a result
a reaction
a decision
a suggestion
the next event
English often uses so, then, or and so, but فَـ does not have one fixed translation.

blocks.heading: The “What follows?” test
paragraphs: When you hear or see فَـ, ask:
“Given the first idea, what follows?”

items.en: The car is broken, so I want a taxi.
The bag is expensive, so I don’t want it.

items.ar: كُلّ الكَراسي مَكْسورة، فَبِدْنا كَراسي جْديدة.
items.translit: kull il-karāsi maksūre, fa-bidna karāsi jdīde.
items.en: All the chairs are broken, so we want new chairs.

items.ar: ما في غُرَف فاضْيِة بِالفُنْدُق، فَبِدْنا فُنْدُق تاني.
items.translit: mā fī ghuraf fāḍye bil-funduʾ, fa-bidna funduʾ tānī.
items.en: There aren’t any available rooms at the hotel, so we want another hotel.

blocks.heading: A Note on Everyday Speech
blocks.text:
فَـ (fa-) is useful to recognize, especially in more structured or formal-sounding Arabic. It connects an idea to what follows, often expressing a result or consequence.
In everyday Palestinian and Jordanian conversation, you're also very likely to hear:
عَشان هيك | so / that's why – ʿashān hēk
مِنشان هيك | so / that's why – minshān hēk

items.ar: السَّيّارة خَرْبانة، عَشان هيك بِدّي تَكْسي.
items.translit: is-sayyāra kharbāne, ʿashān hēk biddī taksī.
items.en: The car is broken, so I want a taxi.

paragraphs: For now, practice عَشان هيك and مِنشان هيك in your own speech. Learn to recognize فَـ when you encounter it.
Remember that فَـ attaches directly to the following word when written.

blocks.heading: فَـ vs عَشان هيك / مِنشان هيك — Which One Should You Use?
paragraphs: All three can sometimes translate as “so,” but they do not feel exactly the same.
عَشان هيك and مِنشان هيك both point back to something already mentioned and introduce its result or consequence.
They can naturally translate as either so or that's why.

فَـ is shorter and more direct. It simply moves from one idea to the result. It is especially useful to recognize in more structured or formal-sounding language. For everyday conversation, start with:
عَشان هيك / مِنشان هيك | so / that's why – ʿashān hēk / minshān hēk
And remember:
فَـ | so / then – fa
The English translations overlap. What matters is recognizing the function of each connector and choosing a form that fits the situation.

blocks.title: OYS Conjunctions Drill: O — Or | Y — Yet | S — So
blocks.instructions:

blocks.heading: 4.7 “A Few” — كم | kam
paragraphs: Now that you’ve learned how to express basic desires and talk about what you have or want, the next useful step is learning how to talk about quantity. You have already encountered plural forms. This pattern gives you another way to say “I want a few…” or “I have some…” using a singular noun.

In this section, we’ll look at one of the most common and useful words for expressing quantity: كَم (kam). With a singular noun, كَم (kam) asks “how many?”, as in كَم وَلَد عِنْدَك؟ (kam walad ʿindak?), “How many children do you have?” But as you’ll see, كَم (kam) is not limited to questions. In everyday speech, it can also be used in statements to express an unspecified quantity.
a few / some — kam | كَم
This word works well after expressions such as biddī, “I want,” and ʿindī, “I have.” It is completely natural in Palestinian and Jordanian Arabic.
We’ll cover broken plurals in depth in Volume Two. For now, this pattern will help you talk about quantities and basic plural ideas using what you already know.

blocks.heading: Usage
paragraphs: Here, kam is used conversationally to mean “a few” or “some” (not as a question word).
Formula: kam + singular indefinite noun = a few items
The noun stays singular in this construction — this is normal and correct in Levantine Arabic. For the pattern taught here, always use كم followed by a singular indefinite noun.

items.en: I have a few things from the store.
I want a few minutes to myself.
I have a few questions for you all.
I have a few days in Amman.

paragraphs: Practice mixing kam with biddī and ʿindī to build natural sentences about what you want or have! This keeps things simple while you’re still getting comfortable with the basics.

lessons.title: Putting It All Together: Everyone Wants Something

blocks.heading: CHAPTER REVIEW — Putting It All Together
paragraphs: In this chapter, you learned how to express what you want using بِدّ (bidd). That’s a major step forward. You can now talk about what you want, what you wanted in the past, and what you will want in the future.
But you’ve learned much more than that. You’ve also practiced identifying specific things, asking questions, expressing quantities, and connecting your ideas to make your Arabic sound more natural.
Let’s review some of the most important structures.

items.en: I want the bag that’s next to the door.

items.ar: شُو نَوْع القَهْوة اللّي بِدَّك إِيّاها؟
items.translit: shū nōʿ il-ʾahwe illī biddak iyyāha?
items.en: What kind of coffee do you want?
I want that apartment, but it’s far away.

items.ar: المَحَلّ مْسَكَّر، عَشان هيك ما في ناس جُوّا.
items.translit: il-maḥall msakkar, ʿashān hēk mā fī nās juwwa.
items.en: The store is closed. That’s why there aren’t any people inside.

paragraphs: Notice how these structures build on one another. You’re no longer limited to saying that you want something. You can explain which one you mean, describe it, talk about its availability, and give reasons for your choices.
That’s how everyday conversations begin to come together.

On the following pages, you’ll see these structures used in a conversation between two brothers, Yezan and Muhammad. You may encounter a few unfamiliar words, and that’s perfectly fine. Don’t worry about understanding every word immediately.
Instead, focus on what you already recognize. Pay attention to how the characters express wants, ask questions, and connect their ideas.
You might be surprised by just how much you can already understand.

blocks.title: Everyone Wants Something
blocks.context:
Setting
Yezan is the oldest of three brothers, so he’s usually the one everyone relies on when something needs to get done.
This morning, Yezan is getting ready to head downtown. Mom has a shopping list, Dad needs a few things, and the youngest brother, Ziyad, has a school field trip coming up.
Before Yezan leaves, Muhammad catches up with him to make sure he knows what everyone needs.

blocks.heading: Dialogue Discussion
paragraphs: Most of the language in this conversation comes from things you’ve already learned. But there are a few expressions and cultural details worth talking about before we finish the chapter.
At the beginning, Mom asks:

items.ar: يا ولاد، شو بدكم من برا؟ يزن بطريقه عالبلد.
items.translit: yā wlād, shū biddkum min barra? Yezan bi-ṭarīʾo ʿal-balad.
items.en: Boys, what do you want from outside? Yezan’s on his way downtown.

paragraphs: In everyday conversation, مِن بَرّا means “from outside.” But here, Mom is asking whether anyone wants Yezan to bring something back while he’s out running errands.

You may also have noticed the expression عَالْبَلَد (ʿal-balad). Although بَلَد can mean “country” or “town,” in places like Amman, البلد often refers to the downtown area or city center. So Yezan isn’t leaving the country. He’s simply heading into town.
Later, Muhammad tells Yezan that Dad wants Turkish coffee with cardamom.

items.en: He wants Turkish coffee with cardamom.

paragraphs: هيل (hēl) means “cardamom,” a fragrant spice commonly added to coffee in Jordan and Palestine.

Coffee is an important part of hospitality throughout the Levant, and you will encounter different preparations depending on the household, café, and occasion. Cardamom is one of the flavors you may notice.
Now, there’s another small expression that Yezan uses after hearing what Mom wants:
ماشي is an extremely common conversational response meaning “okay,” “alright,” or “sounds good.” Depending on how someone says it, it can express agreement, acceptance, or simply acknowledgment.
And finally, we have Yezan’s reaction after hearing everybody’s requests:

items.en: I swear, I need more money!

paragraphs: You’ve probably heard والله (wallāh) before. Literally, it means “by God,” but in everyday conversation, it’s also a very common way to add emphasis. It doesn’t always indicate a serious or formal oath.
The other useful word here is مصاري (maṣāri), which simply means “money.” It’s one of the most common everyday words for money in Palestinian and Jordanian Arabic.

And that brings us to the joke at the end. Yezan is the one running errands, everyone keeps adding something to his list, and by the time Muhammad finishes, Yezan realizes just how much all of this is going to cost.

It’s a simple family conversation, but that’s exactly the point. Most everyday Arabic isn’t built around complicated sentences. It’s built around familiar expressions, practical needs, and people talking to one another.
And you already know how to do quite a bit of that.

blocks.instructions:
Build the Complete Message: 1–5
Use every phrase in each bank once, unchanged. Fill Arabic blanks from right to left; transliteration follows the same phrase order from left to right. Read each completed message aloud.
Build the Complete Message: 6–10
Use every phrase in each bank once. Follow the English meaning.
Build the Complete Message: 11–15
Use every phrase in each bank once. Keep the phrases unchanged and follow the English meaning.
Build the Exchange: 16–20
Use every phrase in each bank once to complete both speakers' lines. Identical phrases are interchangeable.
